title: Modern production is coordinated

blocks.heading: Modern production is coordinated
blocks.text: Modern industrial production can combine machinery, varied inputs and specialised tasks that need coordination. Supporting infrastructure enables production, but naming land, labour and capital is not the same as describing the networks and services connecting activities. Infrastructure includes transport, electricity, water and communication networks. The factors-of-production classification concerns inputs; infrastructure concerns supporting systems. In that input classification, money capital finances resources and capital goods are produced assets used in production, as Topic 3.1 explains. Categories can overlap: a road is a produced asset, yet is discussed as transport infrastructure when its network role matters. Test what the question asks rather than treating the classifications as mutually exclusive lists.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Machinery and advanced technology
blocks.text: Complex machinery and advanced technology can provide control, precision or productive capacity beyond simpler methods. Their productive value depends on suitable tasks, skilled operation, reliable inputs and maintenance. A computer-controlled cutter in an invented garment factory can repeat specified shapes accurately. If no technician can repair a fault, that potential capacity may stand idle. Identify the feature from its productive role, not just the fact that a device looks modern.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Several raw materials
blocks.text: An industrial product can require several raw materials or components whose quantities and quality must fit the process. A shortage of one essential input can interrupt completion even when the other materials are available. A fictional garment producer combines fabric, thread, fasteners and labels. Buying more fabric will not complete an order that lacks suitable fasteners. A wide range of materials means coordination of supply and specifications, not an assertion that every industry requires the same number of inputs.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Specialised industrial tasks
blocks.text: Complex division of labour assigns different specialised tasks or stages to workers and teams. Specialist skills can improve task performance while creating dependence between stages. Designers, cutters, machine operators, quality checkers and dispatch workers perform different roles in a garment process. Naming the total workforce does not show the division. Explain what each relevant stage contributes and how an error in one stage affects the next.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Coordinate the stages
blocks.text: Coordination of specialised tasks arranges the timing, flow and information linking production stages. An unbalanced flow can create queues or idle capacity even when each stage has capable workers. If cutting produces 100 sets a day while stitching completes 60, unfinished sets accumulate unless the imbalance is addressed. Changing schedules, addressing the slow stage or matching output between stages is more useful than simply demanding that cutters work faster.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: An original production comparison
blocks.text: In a fictional factory, cutting capacity is 100 sets daily and stitching completes 60. Completed output is 60 and the unfinished queue grows by 40 sets a day. After a suitable stitching improvement, cutting remains 100 and stitching completes 90, so the queue grows by 10. The smaller imbalance accompanies higher finished output. Faster cutting alone would increase the backlog. Topic 3.1 explains specialised tasks; this example links their flow and coordination to useful industrial output.
